content: Grace Fernald was a prominent educational psychologist who made significant contributions to literacy education in the early 20th century. She is best known for establishing the first clinic for remedial instruction in 1921 at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA). Her work was deeply influenced by tactile learning principles, which can be traced back to figures like Quintilian, Seguin, and Montessori. Fernald developed a kinesthetic method for teaching spelling and reading, which involved students tracing words to reinforce learning. This method became a cornerstone of her research and culminated in her 1943 publication, Remedial Techniques in Basic School Subjects. Her approach continues to influence modern special education and remedial reading practices, and it aligns with Howard Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences, particularly the kinesthetic learning modality. Fernald’s integration of physical, auditory, verbal, and visual elements in reading instruction, now referred to as multimodal or multisensory learning, remains a guiding principle for educators. Grace Maxwell Fernald was born on November 29, 1879, in Clyde, Ohio. She spent her early years in New York and New Jersey before graduating from high school and attending Mt. Holyoke and Bryn Mawr colleges. In 1907, she earned her doctorate in psychology from the University of Chicago. By 1911, she had joined UCLA, where she eventually became the head of the Psychology Department and Laboratory at the State Normal School. It was at UCLA that her groundbreaking research into reading and writing processes gained widespread recognition. In 1921, Fernald published a foundational study in the Journal of Educational Research that detailed her kinesthetic method for teaching four boys with reading difficulties. This method emphasized student choice and involved five distinct phases. In the first phase, students selected focal words, which the teacher wrote on a chalkboard. The students traced the words while repeating them aloud. Once confident, they wrote the words themselves, saying each syllable as they wrote. In the second phase, students created sentences using the same method. The third phase introduced a student-selected book, from which specific words were isolated for practice. In the fourth phase, students read entire phrases from the book, and in the fifth phase, they progressed to silent reading. All four boys in the study successfully learned to read at grade level, and follow-up assessments showed that they maintained or even improved their reading proficiency. Fernald and her co-author Keller noted that the students developed the ability to pronounce new words by analogy, a compensatory strategy still used in modern reading instruction. They also emphasized the importance of individualized instruction and motivation, principles that are evident in contemporary programs like Marie Clay’s Reading Recovery. In 1948, as Fernald prepared to retire from her UCLA clinic after 27 years, Time magazine published an article titled “Reading by Touch,” which highlighted her kinesthetic method. Fernald explained that reading difficulties often stem from an inability to visualize the appearance of words. Her clinic accepted students with average intelligence and required parental commitment to the program, which typically lasted from two months to two years. While the article included some criticisms of her method, it ultimately portrayed her as a dedicated and innovative educator. A former student of Fernald’s clinic, who later became a distinguished doctor and researcher, provided a powerful testimonial in the 1998 edition of the History of Reading News. He described his experiences with the kinesthetic method, including activities like finger painting, and reflected on how Fernald’s approach changed his life. He admitted that he still used aspects of her method in his professional life. His mother also contributed an article to the same publication, recounting how Fernald’s intervention helped their intelligent but struggling second-grade son. She even described a visit to Fernald’s home, emphasizing the personal care and dedication Fernald brought to her work. These accounts highlight the profound impact Fernald had not only on her students but also on their families. When Grace Fernald passed away in 1950, her colleagues celebrated her immense contributions to education. Her work at the UCLA clinic had helped thousands of children and adults, as well as the teachers and psychologists who observed and learned from her methods. Fernald’s legacy endures in the field of literacy education, where her innovative techniques continue to inspire and guide educators.
